verified_claim: Ravimohan et al. describe pulmonary tuberculosis producing destructive lung pathology through caseous necrosis, cavitation and abnormal tissue repair. Caseation destroys alveolar structures and neighbouring tissue, while subsequent healing can produce fibrosis and architectural distortion. Host inflammatory responses and matrix-degrading proteases are implicated in these processes.
limitation_note: Active pulmonary TB can produce tissue destruction and fibrosis, but the extent and type of injury vary considerably. Not every patient develops cavitation or permanent scarring. Specific immune mechanisms are incompletely established and some mechanistic evidence derives from animal models. This source establishes a possible structural injury pathway rather than inevitable permanent lung damage.
review_note: Reviewed Ravimohan et al., Tuberculosis and lung damage: from epidemiology to pathophysiology, particularly Table 1, Granulomas to cavitation during TB and Matrix metalloproteinases. These sections explicitly describe tissue destruction, cavitation and fibrotic repair associated with pulmonary TB. Supports Active pulmonary tuberculosis disease → Lung tissue injury and scarring as a contributory causal relationship. AI-assisted review; human confirmation pending.

verified_claim: The review reports persistent obstructive and restrictive lung-function abnormalities after pulmonary TB and describes associations between structural damage and impairment. Cavities are associated with lower FEV1, bronchiectasis with airflow obstruction, and extensive fibrosis is proposed as an explanation for restrictive ventilatory defects. The authors describe structural remodeling as a probable contributor to post-TB impairment.
limitation_note: Although physiologically plausible mechanisms are discussed, the review does not establish that residual structural damage independently causes later impairment in all cases. Much of the epidemiological evidence is observational, baseline lung function is often unavailable, and the authors acknowledge incomplete understanding of the causal mechanisms. The relation is therefore recorded as ASSOCIATED_WITH rather than a confirmed CAUSES arrow.
review_note: Reviewed Ravimohan et al., particularly Table 1, Variability in lung function deficits, Airflow obstruction and Restrictive ventilatory defects. The article connects cavitation, fibrosis, bronchiectasis and lung remodeling with persistent pulmonary dysfunction, but frequently describes the proposed mechanisms as probable or possible. The structural injury-to-impairment relationship is supported as an association; independent causality is not conclusively established. AI-assisted review; human confirmation pending.

verified_claim: Meghji et al. describe post-tuberculosis lung disease as encompassing residual parenchymal and airway abnormalities, including fibrosis, cavitation and bronchiectasis, alongside persistent respiratory symptoms and impaired lung function. The review reports ongoing abnormalities after completion of TB treatment and recognizes an association between residual structural pathology and post-TB respiratory limitation.
limitation_note: The review explicitly states that causal pathways underlying PTLD remain poorly understood. Structural abnormalities, lung-function impairment and symptoms vary considerably and do not always correlate closely. Smoking, environmental exposures, comorbidities, deconditioning and other factors may contribute to impairment. The source supports association rather than an independently established causal effect of scarring on persistent respiratory limitation.
